item.title: AI Trends Weekly 004 · Always on. Ready to hand over?
item.description: AI is staying at its desk. This week, we ask what it should leave behind so someone else can confidently pick up the work.
item.content:encoded:
AI is staying at its desk. This week, we ask what it should leave behind so someone else can confidently pick up the work.

2026-10-11 – 2026-10-17 · Airing

  1. An always-on computer is not yet a dependable colleague

    This week’s personal agents share a move: taking AI out of a single conversation and giving it a computer that stays online. After you leave, it can organize files, run programs and wake for a scheduled task. Founder Park surveys products living in apps, messages and email, or presented as teams of named bots. Underneath, their foundations increasingly resemble one another: a cloud computer, persistent memory and connections to other tools. 12

  2. Start with a task that can end

    Founder Park points to cancelling subscriptions as a concrete entry point: there is an object and an observable outcome. Compared with “manage my life,” it is easier to check whether a subscription was cancelled, a confirmation arrived and the next bill stopped. One completed, bounded task can give a person a reason to delegate again.

  3. Before adding a team, complete one handoff

    The saved Grok Bot team template separates a chief of staff, feature owners and verifiers. Its useful principle is that the producer cannot approve work merely by declaring it done. Verification should point to inspectable artifacts: a reproduction, test output, screenshots or a run record. The public image shows one template page, not evidence that an entire organizational system has been validated. 06

  4. After a disconnect, “do it again” is not a sufficient recovery policy

    The Pi Durable Objects tutorial provides a lower-level example. It persists conversations, tasks and request receipts, checks repeated requests against previous work, and resumes the original retrieval subtask. The retrieval agent excludes previous retrieval outputs, reducing the risk of a summary becoming evidence for another summary. 30

  5. Scion: the model may not be the first bottleneck

    Anthropic describes an unusual infrastructure change. The company reports daily merges rising from roughly 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September, alongside about 25 million CI checkouts a day. Repeatedly moving history and working copies became a substantial compute and network burden. Scion moves more history queries and merge work to the server, while clients retrieve data needed for the current task. 13

  6. Make the easiest path the correct one

    @poteto’s original post and the saved Chinese explanation prioritize code structure, automated checks, written guidance and human review. I read this as an argument for making interfaces, types and module boundaries expose recurring errors early, instead of repeatedly telling an agent not to make them. 32

  7. Status, sessions and memory preserve different things

    Pi 1.1.0’s Program Status Protocol communicates whether a program is working, blocked or finished. Tern emphasizes persistent sessions across devices. Hy Memory distinguishes chat, work and coding memory. These three product readings need not become three lengthy reports, but they occupy useful positions in a handoff. 05 09 25

  8. Sunday addendum: include the requirements

    Tencent’s engineering article extends AI-assisted development into requirement clarification, technical design, review and organizational knowledge. One concrete mechanism assigns knowledge an expiry date and sends it for re-evaluation; agents can report contradictions with current code. How old answers retire is more useful than a growing knowledge count. 33

  9. IdeaScientist: an idea should have a traceable origin

    Research agents can mistake a large volume of ideas for progress. IdeaScientist separates identifying gaps, retrieving analogous solutions from other fields and developing proposals. Its evaluation limits access to earlier literature and compares proposed directions with later human papers. The saved explanation and original paper remain linked. 07 Paper

  10. Evo²: the improver learns too

    Evo² joins two changes in a loop: editing an agent’s prompts, tools and context organization—its harness—and using those edits and execution outcomes to train the model proposing and diagnosing changes. The contribution connects environmental improvement with model learning, rather than supplying another supposedly magical prompt. 20 Paper

  11. AI studying AI: explanations must risk being wrong

    The saved Synced article describes Nick Cammarata’s interpretability work: one agent proposes an explanation of a neuron, another constructs examples predicted to activate it—or not—and the network tests those predictions. The immediate change is the scale of investigation: more hypotheses can be proposed and challenged. 27

  12. Replication and distillation: separate levels of evidence

    Anthropic’s self-replication study tests setting up inference on different hardware and chaining capabilities in simplified environments. A successful component, a successful controlled sequence and autonomous spread in the real world are distinct claims. Simplified access conditions cannot disappear in the retelling. 11

  13. ExcaliClaw

    A collaborative diagram workspace with storage, collections, sharing and MCP. Keep the discussion editable.

  14. magpie

    One local gateway connects agents, models and accounts. Visible routing makes fallback easier to understand.

  15. mobile-mcp

    Operate iOS and Android simulators or real devices using accessibility trees or screenshot coordinates.

  16. Dots × Blender

    An author uses a persistent computer to make low-poly models and saves the output to Drive. Keep the working files.

  17. JEV 1.14.0

    The update adds image input and box localization. A downstream program can receive a position rather than just prose.

  18. You can take the transcript. Can you take the familiar reply?

    APPSO’s companion-product article raises an overlooked problem through changes in service ownership and operation: a transcript records what already happened. The next reply depends on character settings, the base model, memory selection and service policies. This section considers that product question. Individual bankruptcy and transaction claims in the article have not been independently verified here and are not presented as this issue’s news findings. 17

  19. When functionality is easier to reproduce, what remains?

    Kazik’s article connects cheaper AI-assisted reverse engineering with software defenses and attention. 08 My addition is to distinguish reproducing a feature, operating it reliably and earning continued use. An interface can be imitated; migration, incident handling and confidence in the next upgrade do not disappear as code gets cheaper.

  20. One research desk, two return stories

    The long Opus 5.5 quant-research guide has something more valuable than its “24/7” headline: it asks the reader to fix the research universe, evidence timestamps and arithmetic rules first. A company with listings in several markets must not casually become several companies in the sample. Information learned today cannot enter a historical decision. Only after resolving those issues should AI computation produce comparable results. 03

  21. Sunday addendum: where do beginners learn to review?

    A newly saved APPSO article discusses Anthropic’s internal employment report and a difficult tension: companies increasingly value judgment, yet beginners used to learn judgment through small tasks and mistakes. This is a reading and interpretation of that report, not a causal conclusion about the whole labor market from one company’s hiring changes. 34

  22. Leave a starting point for tomorrow

    One of Lachel’s everyday suggestions connects unexpectedly with the issue: leave a progress note so the next session has an entry point. 01 People forget why they stopped yesterday too. Recording where the work stands, what is blocked and what comes next helps colleagues and agents—and tomorrow’s version of ourselves.

item.title: AI Trends Weekly 003 · OpenAI’s mathematics: progress and resistance
item.description: OpenAI released 700-plus AI mathematics manuscripts. Explore the research, corrections and objections, and how people and AI might collaborate.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI released 700-plus AI mathematics manuscripts. Explore the research, corrections and objections, and how people and AI might collaborate.

2026-10-04 – 2026-10-10 · Airing

  1. AI released 700-plus manuscripts. Why are mathematicians divided?

    On October 6, OpenAI released mathematical research generated by an internal model. Some saw an acceleration of discovery; others called for a boycott. What lies behind these different responses?

  2. Why can an agent forget a request from two hours ago?

    Two Pi engineering articles examine limited working context and the cost of repeatedly processing conversation history.

  3. Can an agent resume after crashing halfway through a task?

    Pi Durable persists work for long-running agents. The difficult case arises when an external action has happened but its result has not yet been recorded.

  4. Dream-RSI: using past experiments to plan the next attempt

    The researchers turn code-optimization history into a replay environment, then use AI to revise the search policy. What does this “dreaming” save?

  5. PANDA: how should a group of agents form a useful team?

    This paper studies collaboration infrastructure: finding suitable partners, organizing communication around a task and continuing when a participant fails.

  6. REA

    Connect a coding agent to application and binary inspection through MCP, tracing how a feature works.

  7. Designeer

    A browsable directory of design tools, components, learning resources and design engineers.

  8. GitAgent

    Keep an agent’s identity, rules, memory and skills in a Git repository, with versioned changes.

  9. Monid

    A shared entry point for agents to discover and call tools through skills, MCP or a CLI.

  10. OpenBot

    Give desktop agents separate instructions and workspaces, with task handoff and shared files.

  11. Rill

    Bring browsing and Claude Code or Codex tasks into one window, connecting pages with project work.

  12. Mintlify

    Help people and agents read, search and use product documentation alongside API workflows.

  13. Lapis One

    A dedicated Debian computer for agents, with remote access and hardware connections to other devices.

  14. vPhone Workstation

    Manage virtual iPhones in a native macOS window, with a device library, settings and lifecycle controls.

  15. T3 Code

    An open-source graphical workspace for coding-agent threads, diffs and Git collaboration.

  16. Turn recurring mistakes into failing checks

    The /correct proposal turns recurring coding mistakes into lint rules, type checks or tests. Even when an agent forgets a verbal correction, the environment can report the same concrete failure. This preserves feedback where the failure condition can be stated clearly.

  17. Names change; project constraints still need clarity

    This reading discusses CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and customization of the environment around an agent. These files serve as project handoffs: how to build, how to validate and which constraints matter. Useful instructions make work startable; filenames and loading behavior remain tool-specific.

  18. EmbeddingGemma 2: one retrieval space across modalities

    Google’s model card describes text, image, video and audio embeddings in a shared 768-dimensional space, with selectively loaded encoders. Try a personal-library task, such as finding an image or recording from text, then evaluate retrieval and device overhead.

  19. The Jev application list keeps growing

    The saved inspection note records awesome-jev growing from 583 to 591 entries, including bisect, moderation and security work. Examine where each decision layer connects and what executes afterward. The count is a snapshot, not a maturity rating.

  20. DEX #366: what computer does a personal agent need?

    DEX groups personal agents, cloud desktops and AI computers. Compare where a task lives: a portable device, an always-on host or a temporary cloud desktop. Start with persistence, data access and recovery needs before choosing hardware or services.

  21. Across 16 products, memory and initiative recur

    Founder Park’s roundup spans personal agents, specialist assistants and memory tools. Use it as a candidate list and try one adjacent to a current task. Useful initiative depends on what a tool remembers, when it interrupts and whether you can inspect and correct it.

  22. Thin Is In: where does control live in a thinner interface?

    Thin Is In connects persistent agents with lighter interfaces. Work that once required opening an app and navigating several controls may begin with a short request. That creates a design question: where do progress, source material and opportunities to take over remain visible?

  23. AIGC Weekly #191: a partial reading

    The cached portion covers personal agents, AI decompilation and cross-device work. The stream reports roughly 21% coverage, so this note retains the excerpt’s threads without presenting a verdict on the entire newsletter. The full issue belongs in its subscription channel.

  24. Does more AI usage mean better value?

    Kazike compares two A16Z reports on usage frequency, payment and concentration of spending. The useful shift is from model capability to how people use AI. Users, paying users and the general population are different denominators. Spending indicates demand; completed tasks, time saved and continued use help explain the value delivered.

  25. The gap between fingers: seeing Zeno’s paradox

    The original post shows a child a finger gap repeatedly halving. Explanation need not begin with complicated notation. Our geometric-series sketch below makes one point: infinitely many remaining steps can have a finite sum; infinitely many steps alone do not imply infinite time.

  26. Hands-On Large Language Models: learn through diagrams

    Jay Alammar and Maarten Grootendorst’s Hands-On Large Language Models connects model concepts to applications through illustrations and code. It provides useful background for this issue: tokens, vector retrieval and generation conditioned on earlier input. Understanding the mechanism makes it easier to locate what a product claim actually changes.

item.title: AI Trends Weekly 002 · Opus 5.5: making films with code
item.description: From films built with code to leaner agents: how do faster, cheaper tools become workflows we can control?
item.content:encoded:
From films built with code to leaner agents: how do faster, cheaper tools become workflows we can control?

2026-09-27 – 2026-10-03 · Airing

  1. Opus 5.5: making films with code

    Opus writes animation, a browser renders frames, and editing tools assemble the film. The interesting change is how precisely a film can be revised.

  2. Stamp-book motion: finish one small gesture

    Page turn, stamp, next page. Study the rhythm and material transitions as UI or brand-motion inspiration; the example does not need a grand AI thesis.

  3. Art history in 15 seconds: expression and compression

    The creator’s Fable 5.5 clip offers visual transitions and stylistic continuity to study. Condensing history is a creative interpretation; a clip alone cannot establish historical accuracy, production time or reproducibility.

  4. Faster technology still needs creative judgment

    Katzenberg brings the discussion back to imagination, emotion and compensation for creators. Alongside the cover story, ask whether easier production also improves storytelling, choices and collaboration terms.

  5. Less context, with evidence intact

    Pi separates the archive from the working context; SoL-Pi reduces repetition. A smaller bill can also come with fewer solved tasks.

  6. Pi Agent 1.0: two paths for agent work

    Pi 1.0 refines the minimal terminal agent; the experimental Pi Durable explores long-running work. The release brings both choices into focus.

  7. Claude Mods: tools that fit your workflow

    From context displays to timely reminders, the terminal agent is becoming a customizable work environment.

  8. From writing code to operating systems

    The Tencent Cloud SRE case connects infrastructure, observations and knowledge in a graph, and stages capability from read-only diagnosis to approved recommendations and execution. The lesson is gradual delegation: demonstrate explanations before permitting operational changes.

  9. Define the work before assembling an agent team

    The Opus team example is a starting point. Decide role boundaries, handoff artifacts and acceptance checks first; independently verifiable work keeps collaboration from merely adding conversation.

  10. When does Jev routing actually save money?

    Five Jev saves explore division of labor: do classification, scoring and routing always require full generative reasoning?

  11. 90.5% at about a fifth of the cost: an eval case

    A 44-ticket support case shows why a higher score needs a named dataset—and an account of what the agent changed.

  12. Bring in an advisor at decision points

    Use the main model for execution and an advisor before a plan, after repeated failures or before completion. This is a community workflow idea; confirm current configuration and model availability rather than using two models for every step.

  13. ElevenLabs

    A hosted platform for narration, dubbing and conversational voice.

  14. VoiceStudio

    A community-recommended local tool for cloning, synthesis and dubbing.

  15. drawgent

    Connect coding agents to a shared Excalidraw canvas.

  16. Chit

    Turn local Claude Code history into project-based receipts.

  17. Hemory

    Convert everyday speech into searchable memory for agents.

  18. NOAN

    A shared source of business facts and context for agents.

  19. Rene

    A personal assistant spanning mobile and shared workflows.

  20. Invent a Dataset

    Generate task-specific training data from an intent.

  21. Maestro

    Describe mobile and web UI tests with readable flows.

  22. e2e · TesterArmy

    Combine deterministic locators and AI steps in one test.

  23. Sonnet 5.5: efficiency for everyday work

    The official launch emphasizes speed and efficiency. Revisit model choice for bounded tasks such as fixes and documents; similar benchmark scores do not mean interchangeable performance on every workload.

  24. DevDay and Jev: decisions as a platform capability

    The two saves summarize DevDay and debate the Decisions API’s impact on Jev. They point toward decisions becoming a platform capability; “killing” a competitor is the author’s interpretation. Compare availability, output guarantees, latency, cost and switching overhead.

  25. DEX #365: what remains scarce when motion is easy?

    This email issue connects ubiquitous motion design with personal agents: lower production barriers do not automatically produce good work, and assistants still need resources and good interactions. It adds an editorial counterpoint to the cover. The saved email has no public original URL.

  26. AIGC #190: an ecosystem snapshot

    The accessible saved portion discusses Opus, Muse and creative examples. This issue indexes only that portion and does not treat the uncaptured paid remainder as read. Alongside DEX, it contrasts new releases with questions about experience and quality.

  27. What does a personal assistant actually save?

    “Nobody wants an AI assistant” is a provocative opinion, not demand data. The useful question is whether users want less mental effort without surrendering decisions. Start with specific repeated tasks and separate recommendations, approvals and execution.

  28. After creation, think about discovery

    This Xiaohongshu marketing save sits at the edge of the AI theme: production also needs discovery and conversion. It remains a short reading note. Timing, account strategy and traffic outcomes are the author’s experience, not guaranteed platform rules.

  29. Behind the “AI ban” headline: terminology

    The executive order concerns using SI instead of AI in applicable executive-branch communications; existing historical documents need not all be revised. The order does not itself ban the technology. Separate terminology, legal definitions and substantive measures before assessing impact.

item.title: AI Trends Weekly 001 · Jev: how should an agent make decisions?
item.description: Inside Jev’s decisions, the next steps in AI creation, Claude’s biology research, and products for everyday life.
item.content:encoded:
Inside Jev’s decisions, the next steps in AI creation, Claude’s biology research, and products for everyday life.

2026-09-20 – 2026-09-26 · Airing

  1. No long answer. How does Jev make a decision?

    Four distinctions matter: a predefined answer space, parallel decisions, probability calibration, and business rules that remain the program’s responsibility.

  2. Pi × Jev：Putting execution authority back into code

    Routing, tool gates and answer verification each address a small question. The model supplies signals; the harness decides the consequences.

  3. Jev and FLock: align the measurement conditions first

    A community test of a thousand financial complaints raises useful questions. Model versions, the distribution of long inputs, network time and cost definitions determine where its conclusions can apply.

  4. Jev’s limitations: turning them into workflow design

    Parallelism pays off only when the task structure suits it. Subtitle selection, date extraction and Chinese-language evaluation reveal the respective boundaries of semantic judgment, deterministic computation and quality assurance.

  5. Four kinds of Jev applications: decisions in real workflows

    Browser, document, advertising and sales demos show different integration patterns. Public code reveals more than demo speed about exactly which step Jev performs.

  6. Tencent’s debugging agent: recommendations need evidence

    Moving from hours to minutes compresses the work of assembling evidence across systems. Read the 88% action-agreement rate alongside the sample’s purpose and its confidence rules.

  7. A one-person Grok business: count review time and failures

    $18K is a revenue target for five clients; the article does not show payment records. Its routing and acceptance design is useful, but operating it requires complete cost accounting and a way to handle exceptions.

  8. Animate the character. Keep the ability to edit it.

    What makes Rege’s example worth saving is the .coa project supplied with the demo. Inside it, expressions, hair movement and timing become separate places to make changes.

  9. A pixel animation in five minutes: what comes after the first result?

    Rikuo’s short clip is a distinctive style reference. Turning it into your own production capability requires visual specifications, editable deliverables and revision tests together.

  10. 463 video examples: turning them into reusable workflows

    The reusable assets are character constraints, storyboard structure and failure records. The post, the repository on the save date and the current repository have different counts. Versions and counting units need to be explicit.

  11. Fish Audio：What can you actually control in a voice?

    Fish Audio’s emotion tags let scripts specify how a line is read. A complete voice workflow still needs reference voices, pronunciation of names, transitions between passages and accounting for repeated generations.

  12. ScreenKite：How conversational editing meets the timeline

    Recording, transcription, editing and B-roll become useful together when every instruction maps to inspectable clips and time ranges. Model costs, asset uploads and editable exports still require separate scrutiny.

  13. Claude found ART. What is actually new?

    AGI Hunt’s report offers a lead more interesting than a model expressing excitement: how much biological understanding advances when a known enzyme, neighboring genes and repeated RNA elements are connected?

  14. After 21 hours: how to review Claude’s research

    AI Era’s 950 agents makes a striking headline. Understanding the actual progress requires separating session counts, candidate counts, report counts and experimental results.

  15. The value of frontline QA: knowing where things break

    A secondhand account of an internal post cannot establish a company’s staffing decisions, but it raises a concrete question: as automation gets cheaper, who defines the real risks worth testing?

  16. Four small products, four everyday obstacles

    Children’s sense of remaining time, adults’ distraction, outdoor exploration and restarting habits all concern time and action, but each needs its own interaction mechanism.
